---

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim-docs/main/getting-started/introduction.md

# Introduction

Feedback Pilgrim is a self-hosted feedback board. Your customers post feature requests, vote and comment on a public site for each of your products. You sort the requests by the revenue of the customers who ask for them.

One instance can hold many projects. Each project has its own public site on a subdomain, for example `acme.feedback.example.com`. The team works in the dashboard on the main domain, for example `feedback.example.com`.

## What you can do

- **Collect feedback.** Contacts post requests, vote and comment on the public site. A contact can attach files to a post and photos to a comment.
- **Organize the work.** Put posts on boards, move them through stages on a kanban board, and add tags. Merge duplicate posts.
- **Weight by revenue.** Send the monthly recurring revenue (MRR) and the lifetime value (LTV) of each contact. The post list can sort by a priority score that adds the MRR of the voters.
- **Show a public roadmap.** The roadmap shows the posts in the stages that you mark for the roadmap.
- **Publish release notes.** Contacts read, vote and comment on them. The widget can open the newest note in your app.
- **Close the loop.** When a post moves to a new stage, the author and the voters get an email.
- **Collect testimonials.** Contacts write testimonials with an optional rating. A testimonial shows on the public site after approval.
- **Embed the widget.** The `pilgrim.js` script signs in the users of your app on the public site, without a second login.
- **Automate.** Use the REST API, the MCP server for AI agents, signed webhooks and Slack messages.
- **Run the instance.** The owner manages the users and the registration mode in the admin area.

## How it works

Feedback Pilgrim is a Laravel 13 app on PHP 8.3, with Blade views, Vue 3 components and Tailwind CSS 4. The main parts are:

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| Web app | Serves the dashboard, the public sites, the widget endpoints, the REST API, the MCP server and the guides at `/documentation`. |
| Database | SQLite in the `/data` volume by default. MySQL 8.4 is also supported. |
| Redis | Optional. With Redis, it holds the cache, the sessions and the queue. Without Redis, the database holds them. |
| Queue worker | Runs `php artisan queue:work`. It sends the emails, the webhooks and the Slack messages. |
| Scheduler | Runs `php artisan schedule:work`. It starts the weekly reports every Monday. |
| File storage | Holds the uploads (attachments, photos, avatars and logos) in `storage/app`. |

Feedback Pilgrim supports SQLite and MySQL 8.4. SQLite is the default, and it is enough for one server. The Docker image runs the web app, the queue worker and the scheduler in one container. PostgreSQL and MariaDB are not tested and not supported.

## Two kinds of accounts

Feedback Pilgrim has two kinds of accounts:

- A **user** signs in to the dashboard with an email and a password. A user can manage one or more projects.
- A **contact** is a customer of one project. A contact signs in to the public site with a signed link, not with a password.

Each user also has an **admin contact** in each of their projects. The admin contact is the identity of the user on the public site and in the MCP tool `create_post_comment`.

## Words that these docs use

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Instance | One installation of Feedback Pilgrim. |
| Owner | A user who runs the instance. Only an owner can open `/admin`. |
| Project | One product with its own public site. The code calls a project a "client". |
| Contact | A customer of a project. |
| Post | One piece of feedback, for example a feature request. |
| Board | A group of posts in a project. |
| Stage | One step of the status pipeline of a post. The dashboard calls a stage a "status". |
| Tag | A label for posts, contacts and release notes. |
| Release note | A changelog entry of a project. |
| Testimonial | A text from a customer, with an optional rating. |
| API token | A personal access token for the REST API and the MCP server. Each token belongs to one project. |
| Publishable key | The public `pk_...` key that the widget sends. It gives no API access. |
| Identity secret | The secret that your server uses to sign the email of a user for the widget. |

# Install with Docker

Feedback Pilgrim runs in one container. The container serves the app, runs the queue worker and the scheduler, and keeps all the data in one volume at `/data`. The default database is SQLite. You need no `.env` file.

## Try it on your computer

```bash
docker run -d --name feedbackpilgrim -p 8080:8080 -v feedbackpilgrim:/data ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim
docker logs -f feedbackpilgrim
```

The last line of the log is the setup URL, for example `http://localhost:8080/setup?token=...`. Open it, then create the owner account and the first project.

The public site of a project is at `http://<subdomain>.localhost:8080`. Browsers send `*.localhost` to your own computer, so you need no DNS record.

## Install on a server

You need:

- A Linux server with Docker, on amd64 or arm64. 1 GB of memory is enough.
- Ports 80 and 443 open to the internet.
- A domain for the dashboard, for example `feedback.example.com`.

1. Add two DNS A records that point to the IP address of the server:

   | Name | What it serves |
   |---|---|
   | `feedback.example.com` | The dashboard, the REST API, the MCP server and `pilgrim.js` |
   | `*.feedback.example.com` | The public site of each project |

2. Run the installer on the server:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/main/install.sh | bash
   ```

3. Type the domain when the installer asks for it.
4. Open the setup URL that the installer shows.
5. Create the owner account and the first project. Then the app signs you in.

The installer checks Docker, the CPU architecture and the ports. It starts the container, waits until the app answers, and shows the setup URL. It writes a log to `/tmp/feedbackpilgrim-install.log`.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--domain=<host>` | Uses this domain. The installer does not ask. |
| `--non-interactive` | Asks nothing. The installer reads the domain from `APP_DOMAIN`. |
| `--dry-run` | Prints each docker command. The installer changes nothing. |

To pass an option through `curl`, use `bash -s --`, for example `curl -fsSL <url> | bash -s -- --dry-run`.

## Start the container without the installer

```bash
docker run -d --name feedbackpilgrim --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 80:80 -p 443:443 -p 443:443/udp \
  -e APP_DOMAIN=feedback.example.com \
  -v feedbackpilgrim:/data \
  ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim
```

When `APP_DOMAIN` is set, the container serves ports 80 and 443 with automatic HTTPS. Read [Reverse proxy and TLS](../self-hosting/reverse-proxy-and-tls.md).

The image tag `latest` is the latest release. To stay on one version, use a version tag, for example `ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim:0.1.0`.

## The setup URL

The setup page at `/setup` creates the owner account and the first project. It is open only while the instance has no user.

The setup URL holds a token. The app makes the token from `APP_KEY` with HMAC-SHA256, so the instance stores no token. If you open `/setup` without the correct token, the page shows no form. It shows the commands that print the setup URL, and a field for the token.

If you lose the setup URL, show it again:

```bash
docker exec feedbackpilgrim php artisan fp:setup-url
```

After the first user exists, `/setup` sends you to the login page.

## Create the owner from the command line

An agent or a script can create the owner without the setup page:

```bash
docker exec feedbackpilgrim php artisan fp:install \
  --name="Ada Lovelace" --email=ada@example.com \
  --project="Acme" --subdomain=acme \
  --json --no-interaction
```

The command returns a `login_url` that works one time, for 60 minutes. With `--with-token=<name>`, it also makes an API token and returns the commands that connect an AI agent. A second run with the same email makes no change and returns `"status":"exists"`. Read [Accounts and registration](../self-hosting/accounts-and-registration.md).

## What the container does at start

1. On the first start, it makes `APP_KEY` and the other secrets. It writes them to a file in `/data` with mode 600. On each later start, it reads the same file.
2. It runs the migrations.
3. It starts the web server, the queue worker and the scheduler.
4. If no account exists, it prints the setup URL as the last line of the log. If an owner exists, it prints the app URL.

The Docker health check calls `/up`.

## The `/data` volume

The volume holds all the data of the instance:

- the SQLite database
- the generated secrets, with `APP_KEY`
- the uploads: post attachments, comment photos, avatars and logos
- the TLS certificates

WARNING: Back up the `/data` volume. If you lose it, you lose `APP_KEY`, and a restored database cannot decrypt the identity secrets of the projects. Read [Backups](../self-hosting/backups.md).

## Environment variables

On localhost, the container needs no variable. On a server, `APP_DOMAIN` is the only required variable. The app derives `APP_URL`, `SESSION_DOMAIN`, `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS` and `SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE` from it.

To set more values, add `-e NAME=value` to `docker run`, or use `--env-file`. Read [Configuration](configuration.md) for all the variables, and [Mail](../self-hosting/mail.md) for the mail server.

## MySQL and Redis

The repository has a `docker-compose.yml` for MySQL 8.4 and Redis 7.4. Use it if you already run MySQL, or if you want the database in a separate container.

1. Clone the repository and go into its folder:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim.git
   cd feedbackpilgrim
   ```

2. Copy the example environment file:

   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

3. In `.env`, set `APP_DOMAIN` and `DB_PASSWORD`.
4. In `.env`, remove the `#` from the lines of the "MySQL and Redis" block. The block sets `COMPOSE_PROFILES=mysql`, so Compose also starts the `mysql` and `redis` services.
5. Build and start the stack:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

6. Read the setup URL on the last line of the log:

   ```bash
   docker compose logs -f web
   ```

Without step 4, the same Compose file runs the `web` service with SQLite. The `web` service runs the app, the queue worker and the scheduler. A fresh MySQL install loads a schema dump, so the first start is fast. The `web` service waits for MySQL before it runs the migrations.

The Compose file publishes port 8080 on `127.0.0.1` and expects your own proxy with TLS. To let the container get its own certificates, set `CADDY_ENABLED=true` and publish ports 80 and 443. To use the published image instead of a local build, use `docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml`.

## Next steps

- [Configuration](configuration.md)
- [Reverse proxy and TLS](../self-hosting/reverse-proxy-and-tls.md)
- [Backups](../self-hosting/backups.md)
- [Upgrading](upgrading.md)
- [Connect an AI agent](../mcp/connecting-clients.md)

# Install without Docker

This page installs Feedback Pilgrim on a Linux server with PHP and a web server. The Docker image is faster to install and does these steps for you. Read [Install with Docker](installation-docker.md).

## Requirements

| Item | Version or detail |
|---|---|
| PHP | 8.3 or later (`composer.json` requires `^8.3`) |
| PHP extensions | `pdo_sqlite` or `pdo_mysql`, `gd`, `exif`, `pcntl`, `opcache` and `zip`. Add `redis` if you use Redis. The Docker image has these extensions. |
| Composer | 2 |
| Node.js | 24, to build the assets. The server does not need Node.js after the build. |
| A database | SQLite 3, or MySQL 8.4. For SQLite, the `sqlite3` binary must also be installed. |
| Redis | Optional. The Compose stack uses Redis 7.4. |
| A web server | Its document root must be the `public/` folder. |

Without Redis, set `CACHE_DRIVER`, `SESSION_DRIVER` and `QUEUE_CONNECTION` to `database`. With Redis, the app uses the `phpredis` client (`REDIS_CLIENT=phpredis`), so PHP needs the `redis` extension.

The [`deploy/`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/tree/main/deploy) folder of the app repository has example files for an install without Docker:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`nginx/feedbackpilgrim.conf`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/deploy/nginx/feedbackpilgrim.conf) | NGINX with PHP-FPM |
| [`caddy/Caddyfile`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/deploy/caddy/Caddyfile) | Caddy with PHP-FPM |
| [`systemd/feedbackpilgrim-queue.service`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/deploy/systemd/feedbackpilgrim-queue.service) | The queue worker as a systemd service |
| [`systemd/feedbackpilgrim-scheduler.service`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/deploy/systemd/feedbackpilgrim-scheduler.service) | The scheduler as a systemd service |
| [`supervisor/feedbackpilgrim.conf`](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/deploy/supervisor/feedbackpilgrim.conf) | The queue worker and the scheduler as Supervisor programs |

The files use the app folder `/var/www/feedbackpilgrim`, the user `www-data` and the PHP-FPM socket `/run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock`. Replace these values with the values of your server.

## Install

1. Clone the repository and go into its folder:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim.git
   cd feedbackpilgrim
   ```

2. Install the PHP packages without the development packages:

   ```bash
   composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
   ```

3. Build the dashboard assets and the widget:

   ```bash
   npm ci
   npm run build
   ```

   The build makes `public/build` and `public/pilgrim.js`.

4. Copy the example environment file and make the app key:

   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   php artisan key:generate
   ```

5. Set the values in `.env`. Read [Configuration](configuration.md).
6. Create the tables:

   ```bash
   php artisan migrate --force
   ```

7. Create the storage link:

   ```bash
   php artisan fp:install --prepare
   ```

8. Cache the configuration, the routes and the views:

   ```bash
   php artisan optimize
   ```

9. Configure the web server. Send the dashboard domain and the wildcard of the projects to `public/index.php`. Start from the NGINX or the Caddy example above.
10. Give the user of the web server write access to `storage/` and `bootstrap/cache/`.
11. Start the queue worker and the scheduler. Read [Queues and the scheduler](../self-hosting/queues-and-scheduler.md).

## Create the owner

To get the setup URL, run:

```bash
php artisan fp:setup-url
```

Open the URL. Create the owner account and the first project.

To create the owner in the terminal instead, run:

```bash
php artisan fp:install
```

Read [Accounts and registration](../self-hosting/accounts-and-registration.md) for the options of `fp:install`.

## After a change to `.env`

`php artisan optimize` caches the configuration. If you change `.env` after that, the app does not see the change.

1. Run `php artisan optimize` again.
2. Restart the queue worker with `php artisan queue:restart`.

## Next steps

- [Configuration](configuration.md)
- [Reverse proxy and TLS](../self-hosting/reverse-proxy-and-tls.md)
- [Queues and the scheduler](../self-hosting/queues-and-scheduler.md)

# Configuration

Feedback Pilgrim reads its configuration from environment variables. The file `.env.example` in the repository explains each value. This page lists the values that an instance needs.

The Docker image needs no variable on localhost. On a server, `APP_DOMAIN` is the only required variable. The image makes `APP_KEY` on the first start and keeps it in the `/data` volume.

To set a variable:

- With `docker run`, add `-e NAME=value` or `--env-file <file>`. Then remove the container and start it again with the same volume.
- With Docker Compose, put the value in `.env`. Then run `docker compose up -d`.
- Without Docker, put the value in `.env`. Then run `php artisan optimize` and `php artisan queue:restart`.

To see the values that the app uses, run `php artisan fp:status --json`. To find a wrong value, run `php artisan fp:doctor`.

## Domains

The app has two kinds of hosts:

- The **app host** is the host of `APP_URL`. It serves the dashboard, the login pages, the admin area, the guides at `/documentation`, the REST API and the MCP server.
- Each **project** has a public site on a subdomain of `APP_DOMAIN`, for example `acme.feedback.example.com`.

The app finds the project from the subdomain. The app host and `APP_DOMAIN` itself are never a project. A reserved subdomain (for example `www` or `api`) is never a project.

`APP_DOMAIN` can be the same as the app host, or its parent. For example, the dashboard can be on `app.example.com` and the projects on `<slug>.example.com`.

| Variable | Example | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `APP_URL` | `https://feedback.example.com` | The full URL of the dashboard. Its scheme (`http` or `https`) is also the scheme of the public sites. |
| `APP_DOMAIN` | `feedback.example.com` | The base domain of the public sites. The DNS needs a wildcard record for it. |
| `SESSION_DOMAIN` | `.feedback.example.com` | The leading dot shares the dashboard session with the project subdomains. The **Public Site** link of the dashboard needs it. |
| `SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE` | `true` | Set `true` when `APP_URL` uses `https`. |
| `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS` | `feedback.example.com,*.feedback.example.com` | The domains that can call the API with the session cookie. List the dashboard domain and the wildcard of the projects. |

Set only `APP_DOMAIN`. The app derives the other four values from it: `APP_URL` is `https://<APP_DOMAIN>`, and the cookie and Sanctum values cover the domain and its wildcard. If you set `APP_URL`, the app derives the values from `APP_URL` instead. Set a value yourself only to change the derived value.

The app trusts the `X-Forwarded-*` headers from any proxy. Read [Reverse proxy and TLS](../self-hosting/reverse-proxy-and-tls.md).

## Application

| Variable | Default in `.env.example` | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `APP_NAME` | `"Feedback Pilgrim"` | The name of the app in the pages and the emails. |
| `APP_ENV` | `production` | The environment. Use `local` for development. |
| `APP_KEY` | empty | The encryption key. The Docker image makes it on the first start and keeps it in `/data`. Without Docker, make it with `php artisan key:generate --show`. |
| `APP_DEBUG` | `false` | Shows error details. Keep it `false` in production. |
| `REGISTRATION_ENABLED` | `false` | The default registration mode. `true` is open, `false` is closed. Read [Accounts and registration](../self-hosting/accounts-and-registration.md). |

WARNING: Make a backup of `APP_KEY`. The app uses it to encrypt the identity secret of each project and to sign the sign-in links of the contacts. If the key changes, the stored identity secrets cannot be read, and the old links stop working.

## Database

| Variable | Default in `.env.example` |
|---|---|
| `DB_CONNECTION` | `mysql` |
| `DB_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` |
| `DB_PORT` | `3306` |
| `DB_DATABASE` | `feedbackpilgrim` |
| `DB_USERNAME` | `feedbackpilgrim` |
| `DB_PASSWORD` | empty |

The Docker image uses SQLite by default. The database file is in the `/data` volume. SQLite is enough for one server.

To use MySQL, set `DB_CONNECTION=mysql` and the other `DB_*` values. The Compose file of the repository starts MySQL 8.4 with the `mysql` profile and sets `DB_HOST` and `DB_PORT`. Read [Install with Docker](installation-docker.md#mysql-and-redis).

## Redis, cache, sessions and queue

| Variable | Default in `.env.example` | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `REDIS_CLIENT` | `phpredis` | The Redis client. |
| `REDIS_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | The Redis host. |
| `REDIS_PASSWORD` | `null` | The Redis password. |
| `REDIS_PORT` | `6379` | The Redis port. |
| `CACHE_DRIVER` | `redis` | The cache store. |
| `QUEUE_CONNECTION` | `redis` | The queue. Read [Queues and the scheduler](../self-hosting/queues-and-scheduler.md). |
| `SESSION_DRIVER` | `redis` | The session store. |
| `SESSION_LIFETIME` | `120` | The session lifetime in minutes. |

Redis is optional. Without Redis, the Docker image keeps the cache, the sessions and the queue in the database. The Compose file with the `mysql` profile also starts Redis 7.4.

## Logging

| Variable | Default in `.env.example` | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `LOG_CHANNEL` | `stack` | The log channel. |
| `LOG_STACK` | `daily` | A comma-separated list of channels. Use `stderr` with Docker. Add `rollbar` to send errors to Rollbar. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | The lowest level that the log keeps. |
| `ROLLBAR_TOKEN` | empty | The access token of Rollbar. |

## Mail

SMTP is the default mailer. Mailgun and Amazon SES are optional. Read [Mail](../self-hosting/mail.md) for the variables.

## Files

The uploads go to the `public` disk, that is `storage/app/public`, through the storage link `public/storage`. `FILESYSTEM_DISK` is `local` in `.env.example`.

The app does not support S3 storage for the uploads. The configuration has an `s3` disk, but the S3 driver needs the package `league/flysystem-aws-s3-v3`. The app does not include this package, so each read or write on the `s3` disk fails. Do not set `FILESYSTEM_DISK` or `MEDIA_DISK` to `s3`.

## Docker only

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `CADDY_ENABLED` | `auto` | `auto` starts Caddy with automatic HTTPS only when `APP_DOMAIN` is set. `true` always starts it. `false` never starts it, for example behind your own proxy. The Compose files set `false`. |
| `ACME_EMAIL` | empty | Optional. Let's Encrypt sends notices about the certificates to this address. |

## Docker Compose only

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `APP_PORT` | `8080` | The port of the host that Compose publishes for the `web` service. |
| `APP_BIND` | `127.0.0.1` | The interface of the host for `APP_PORT`. With `127.0.0.1`, only a proxy on the same host can reach the app. Set `0.0.0.0` to accept traffic from other hosts. |

---

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim-docs/main/getting-started/upgrading.md

# Upgrading

Only the latest release gets security fixes. The changelog of the app repository lists the changes and the breaking changes of each version. Read it before you upgrade. The [release notes](release-notes.md) list the changes that users can see, by date.

You can skip versions, for example from `0.1.0` to `0.3.0`. `php artisan migrate` runs all the migrations that the instance does not have, in order. Read the changelog of each version that you skip, because a version can have a manual step.

Make a backup before you upgrade. Read [Backups](../self-hosting/backups.md).

## Upgrade the container

Run the installer again. It downloads the new image and replaces the container. The data in the volume stays.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/main/install.sh | bash
```

To upgrade without the installer:

1. Get the new image:

   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim
   ```

2. Remove the old container. The volume stays:

   ```bash
   docker rm -f feedbackpilgrim
   ```

3. Start the container with the same `docker run` command as before.

The container runs the new migrations when it starts. Run `docker exec feedbackpilgrim php artisan fp:doctor` after the upgrade.

## Upgrade with Docker Compose

1. Get the new code:

   ```bash
   git pull
   ```

2. Build the image and start the stack again:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

The `web` service runs the new migrations when it starts. The `queue` and `scheduler` services start again after `web` is healthy.

## Upgrade with the published image

1. If `.env` sets `FEEDBACKPILGRIM_VERSION`, change it to the new version.
2. Get the new image:

   ```bash
   docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml pull
   ```

3. Start the stack again:

   ```bash
   docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml up -d
   ```

## Upgrade without Docker

1. Get the new code:

   ```bash
   git pull
   ```

2. Install the PHP packages:

   ```bash
   composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
   ```

3. Build the assets and the widget:

   ```bash
   npm ci
   npm run build
   ```

4. Run the new migrations:

   ```bash
   php artisan migrate --force
   ```

5. Cache the configuration, the routes and the views again:

   ```bash
   php artisan optimize
   ```

6. Restart the queue worker:

   ```bash
   php artisan queue:restart
   ```

## If an upgrade fails

Restore the backup that you made before the upgrade. Do not use `php artisan migrate:rollback`. Some migrations change or remove data, and their `down` method cannot bring the data back. For example, the migration that adds the unique index of the votes removes the duplicate votes.

1. Stop the queue worker and the scheduler.
2. Go back to the old version of the code or the image.
3. Restore the database, `storage/app` and `.env` from the backup. Read [Backups](../self-hosting/backups.md).
4. Start the app again.

## Instances made with older code

These notes apply to an instance that existed before some changes in the code.

### The owner flag

The migration `2026_11_17_000100_add_is_owner_to_users_table` makes the first user (the lowest id) the owner. If that user is not the person who runs the instance, make the correct user an owner:

```bash
php artisan fp:install --promote=person@example.com
```

### The old billing step

The migration `2026_11_16_000001_complete_pricing_onboarding` moves users from the old `pricing` onboarding step to `completed`. Feedback Pilgrim has no billing now. An instance that ran the old billing migrations keeps the unused `subscriptions` tables and the billing columns of `users`.

### Identity verification of the widget

A new project requires identity verification of the widget. A project that existed before this setting does not require it. Read [The embeddable widget](../using-feedback-pilgrim/widget.md#identity-verification).

### The old widget key

The widget sends the publishable key (`pk_...`) of the project. The app accepts only this key. A host app that still sends the old public widget token gets `401` with the error `Invalid client key`, and the widget does not load.

CAUTION: Update each host app before you upgrade. Put the publishable key from **Settings > Embed Widget** in the `data-client` attribute of the script tag.

### The testimonial rating setting

The app creates the testimonial settings for each new project. To create the rating setting for projects that do not have it, run:

```bash
php artisan setup:testimonial-rating-settings
```

### The custom attributes of contacts

The app makes the list of custom attributes from the metadata of the contacts. To make the list again from all the contacts, run:

```bash
php artisan fp:sync-contact-attributes
```

---

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim-docs/main/getting-started/release-notes.md

# Release notes

This page lists the changes to Feedback Pilgrim that users can see. The newest date is first. Each date is the day that the change merged into the `main` branch of the app (UTC).

This page is about the Feedback Pilgrim app itself. To publish the release notes of your own project, read [Release notes](../using-feedback-pilgrim/release-notes.md).

A version heading marks the day of a release. The changes in the dated entries below a version heading are part of that version. For developers, `CHANGELOG.md` in the [app repository](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) lists the changes to the code for each version.

## November 25, 2026: version 0.1.0

Version 0.1.0 is the first public release of Feedback Pilgrim. The [GitHub release](https://github.com/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim/releases/tag/v0.1.0) lists all the changes. The Docker image is `ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim:0.1.0`. Read [Install with Docker](installation-docker.md).

With this version, you can:

- Collect feedback on boards, with posts, votes, comments, tags and stages. A project can have more than one board.
- Give each project a public site on its own subdomain, with the posts, the roadmap, the release notes and the testimonials.
- Sort the requests by revenue, with the MRR and the LTV of each contact.
- Publish release notes, and tell the voters of a request when it ships.
- Collect testimonials with a rating, and approve each testimonial before it shows.
- Put the widget (`pilgrim.js`) in your app. It signs in your users with a publishable key and an HMAC `userHash`.
- Connect other apps through the REST API, the signed webhooks and Slack. Connect AI assistants through the MCP server.
- Get a weekly report each Monday.
- Run Feedback Pilgrim on your own server with Docker, or without Docker with the example files in `deploy/`.
- Choose open or closed registration, deactivate users, and recover access with the `fp:user:list` and `fp:user:password` commands.

The changes of November 25, 2026:

- A new install takes one command. If you open the setup page without the setup URL, the page tells you how to find it.
- The Docker image starts with no settings. It uses SQLite, makes its own app key, and runs the queue worker and the scheduler in the same container. Set `APP_DOMAIN` to get automatic HTTPS from the built-in Caddy server.
- An AI agent can install and run Feedback Pilgrim from the command line. Each `fp:` command has a `--json` mode. `fp:install` returns a one-time login link and an MCP token.
- A new API token has scoped access (REST API, MCP read, MCP write) and an optional expiry date.
- On the contact edit page, **Remove field** now removes only the selected custom field. Before, it also hid the next field, and a save lost its value.

## November 24, 2026

- A **Settings > Email** page. A project can send the emails to its contacts from its own domain through Amazon SES. The page shows the DNS records, and the app checks a pending domain every 10 minutes. Until SES verifies the domain, the emails come from `MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS`. Read [Send email from your domain](../using-feedback-pilgrim/sending-domain.md).
- The new `AWS_SES_*` values are optional. If one is empty, the app uses the matching `AWS_*` value. Read [Mail](../self-hosting/mail.md#amazon-ses).
- An **Import** button on the **Testimonials** page. It imports a CSV export from Senja. Each row with text becomes an approved testimonial. Read [Testimonials](../using-feedback-pilgrim/testimonials.md#import-testimonials-from-senja).
- The public site and the dashboard have a new layout, new menus and new empty states. The pages, the fields and the texts stay the same. The mobile menus and the filter panels close on Escape.
- The `LICENSE` file. Feedback Pilgrim is under the GNU Affero General Public License version 3 (AGPL-3.0).
- Example files in `deploy/` for an install without Docker: NGINX, Caddy, systemd and Supervisor. An NGINX example for a proxy in front of the Docker stack.
- The default image in `docker-compose.image.yml` is `ghcr.io/amedina068/feedbackpilgrim`.
- The **Delete Account** button on the profile page opened nothing. It now opens the dialog that asks for the password.
- The "Saved." message on the profile page stayed on the page. It now goes away after two seconds.

## November 18, 2026

- The OpenAPI spec in `docs/api/openapi.yaml`, with the widget `init` call and the key that each operation needs. A Postman collection and environment are in `docs/api/`.
- Each webhook request has `X-FeedbackPilgrim-Timestamp` and `X-FeedbackPilgrim-Signature-V2`, an HMAC-SHA256 of `timestamp.body`. Receivers can reject an old or replayed request.
- Each webhook request has an `X-FeedbackPilgrim-Delivery` ID. Each retry sends the same ID.
- An edit page for a release note in the dashboard. Before, the **Edit** link returned 404.
- A **Settings > Project** page to change the name, the website and the logo of a project.
- A **New project** item in the project selector. It opens the form for a new project.
- Rename and delete a tag on its page in the dashboard. A delete removes the tag from posts, contacts and release notes.
- The Compose files publish the port of the `web` service on `127.0.0.1` by default. Set `APP_BIND=0.0.0.0` to accept traffic from other hosts.
- The Postman link on the API Tokens settings page downloads the collection that the spec makes (`/documentation/postman/download`). The old hand-made collection in `public/` is removed.
- `published_at` is the only publication switch of a release note. **Publish** sets the date if it is empty, and **Unpublish** clears it. The create form has no status field. Leave the date empty to save a draft. A migration copies the old status into `published_at` and removes the `status` column.
- The release note operations of the REST API and the MCP server accept `published` (boolean). The responses have no `status` field.
- A status change from the REST API or the MCP server now sends the same emails, webhooks and Slack message as a stage change in the dashboard.
- Removed: the lookup of the `custom_domain` client setting. Nothing in the app set it, and custom domains are not supported. A host outside `APP_DOMAIN` gets 404.
- Deprecated: the `X-FeedbackPilgrim-Signature` webhook header signs the body only. The next release removes it. Verify `X-FeedbackPilgrim-Signature-V2` instead.
- The API reference showed the wrong pagination fields. It now shows the Laravel paginator that the API returns.
- `GET /api/public/v1/testimonials?approved=false` returned the approved testimonials. It now returns the pending testimonials.
- The testimonial list of the REST API and the MCP server had no order without `sort_by`. It now lists the newest testimonials first.
- The widget `init` call returned 500 when `releaseNotes` had no `show` key. `show` is now optional.
- The widget never opened the newest release note by itself. The init call checked the note two times, and the second check always said "seen". The widget now opens a new note one time for each contact.
- **Unarchive** in the dashboard changed the first post of the project, not the post on the page. It now changes the post on the page.
- The **Publish** and **Unpublish** buttons of a release note returned 500. They now publish and unpublish the note, with a correct message.
- A tag delete from the REST API or the MCP server kept the links from the tag to release notes. It now removes them, as the spec says.
- The weekly report of Monday 09:00 covered the week that started on the same day, so it held only nine hours. It now covers the previous week, Monday to Sunday.
- `GET /posts?sort_by=<unknown value>` on the public site returned 500, and the value went into the SQL `ORDER BY`. The page now accepts only its four sorts. Another value shows the newest posts.
- The project form refused an empty website, because the `domain` rule referred to itself. An empty website now removes the "Back to" link of the public site.
- After an `APP_KEY` change, the widget settings page, the **Regenerate secret** button and each widget `init` call with a `userHash` returned 500. The page now says that the app cannot read the secret, the button makes a new secret, and the widget refuses the hash with 403.
- Feedback Pilgrim loads no analytics script on its pages. The app sends no page views to an outside service.
- A post on a private board no longer shows on the public site, and its URL gets 404. Contacts cannot vote for or comment on a post on a private board or on a draft post. To show a board, mark it public on the Boards page.
- The URL of a draft release note gets 404.
- A webhook URL must use https and point to a public address. An existing webhook with an http URL or a private address stops. Change it to a public https URL.
- A webhook endpoint that answers with a redirect now fails. Enter the final URL of the endpoint.
- A contact has one vote for each item. The update removes duplicate votes, so some vote counts go down.
- The public site and the widget limit the posts, comments, testimonials and votes of each contact and of each IP address. Over the limit, the app answers 429.
- The REST API allows 120 requests each minute for each user or IP address. Before, it allowed 1000.
- The widget `init` call accepts only a publishable key that starts with `pk_`. Another value gets 401.
- Identity verification matches an email only when it is the same after the app removes spaces and changes it to lowercase. An email that differs only by an accent makes a new contact.
- A new project logo gets a random file name and a new URL.
- If an owner removes a user from a project, the dashboard of that user opens the next project of the user.

## November 17, 2026

- Billing is removed. Onboarding has no pricing step, and it goes to the dashboard.
- Registration is off by default. Set `REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true` to turn it on. A password for a new account must have 8 characters or more.
- A new instance opens a setup page. The page creates the owner, the first project and the admin contact. `php artisan fp:setup-url` prints its URL.
- `php artisan fp:install` creates the owner, the first project and the admin contact from the command line. It runs only on an empty database.
- The owner has an admin area at `/admin`. It lists the users, and it can deactivate and reactivate a user. It also sets the registration mode, open or closed.
- A deactivated user cannot sign in, and the API tokens of the user stop working. The data of the user stays.
- `php artisan fp:user:list` lists the users. `php artisan fp:user:password` sets a new password for a user.
- Feedback Pilgrim runs with Docker Compose: the web server, the queue worker, the scheduler, MySQL and Redis.
- The release notes widget shows the name of its own project. Before, it showed the same name for every project.
- The dashboard runs on the host of `APP_URL`. The public sites of the projects stay on subdomains of `APP_DOMAIN`.
- A new project cannot use a reserved subdomain, for example `admin`, `api`, `app` or `www`.
- Contact sign-in links now expire. A link on a page works for 24 hours, and a link in an email works for 7 days. An older link opens the public board without a sign-in.
- Without a `userHash`, the widget signs in only a new contact. For a returning contact, it opens the public board without a sign-in. To sign in returning users, send a `userHash`.
- An API token works only when its user is a member of the project of the token. Other tokens get 401 on the REST API and the MCP server.
- A Markdown link with an unsafe scheme, for example `javascript:`, shows as text.
- Post attachments and comment photos get a random file name with the extension of their file type. The pages show the original name.
- The testimonial widget takes the contact from a signed token. Without a valid token, the testimonial is anonymous. Each IP address can send 5 testimonials each minute.

## November 16, 2026

- The widget uses a publishable key that starts with `pk_`. The embed snippet has no API token. **Settings > Embed Widget** shows the key, the snippet and the identity secret.
- The widget `init` call accepts a `userHash`, an HMAC-SHA256 of the email of the user. A wrong hash gets 403. New projects require the hash.
- The old values of the embed snippet no longer work as tokens for the REST API and the MCP server. The widget accepted them until November 18, 2026.
- The widget `init` call without a contact email now returns 422 with an error message. Before, it returned 500.
- `pilgrim.js` sends its requests to the host that served the script. One build of the script works on more than one host.

## September 25, 2026

- Feedback Pilgrim can send email through Amazon SES. Set `MAIL_MAILER=ses`, then set the AWS access key, the secret key and the region.

## September 10, 2026

- The MCP server has a new tool, `create_post_comment`. It adds a comment to a post as the user of the API token. The author of the post gets an email.

## June 16, 2026

- The project logo upload accepts JPG, PNG, GIF and WebP files. It refuses SVG files. SVG logos that are already stored still show.

## February 11, 2026

- A REST API for posts, contacts, release notes, tags and testimonials. Make an API key in the settings to use it.

## August 7, 2025

- When a post moves to completed, Feedback Pilgrim can ask the author of the post for a testimonial by email. Turn on the testimonial automation in the settings, and write the text of the email. A contact who already gave a testimonial gets no email.
